title: Design
intro: Write down what the shelf API answers before anyone builds it, in the Design room's forms: its entities and relations, its endpoints with their refusals, and one decision with its reason.
taskPanel:
Design: the shelf's contract

Before anyone writes code, write down what the API answers. Fill the design in the Design room's forms: the entities and operations on the UML model tab, the endpoints and the error catalogue on the API contract tab, and one decision with its reason.

What good looks like

- The entities the shelf is made of, such as a book and its loan, with their attributes, and the relations that join them.
- An endpoint for every operation a story needs: the method, the path and what it answers.
- Every refusal on its endpoint, with its status and the error code in its body: a book nobody has, a book already on loan, a book that is not on loan.
- One decision in the decision log, the alternative you rejected and the reason it lost.

Using the AI mentor well

Ask the mentor what a client would need to know to call each endpoint, then check your design against that list yourself.
objectives: List every operation the API answers
Name the status and error code of every refusal
Record one decision, the alternative and the reason

criteria.title: Contract
criteria.description: Every operation the stories need, and every refusal with its status and error code, as a client would need them.

criteria.title: Decision
criteria.description: A decision, the alternative it beat and the reason.

criteria.title: Completeness
criteria.description: Every story the design lists is served by an operation, and every operation names its inputs and what it returns.

stories.title: Browse the shelf
stories.line: As a member, I want to see every book in shelf order, so that I can find one without asking.

stories.title: Lend a book
stories.line: As a librarian, I want to record who has borrowed a book, so that I know where it is.

stories.title: Return a book
stories.line: As a librarian, I want to put a returned book back, so that the next member can borrow it.

assistant.systemPrompt: You are the LearnSDLC mentor for the DESIGN phase of Shelf, a teacher's own application: a Python Flask API that keeps books in memory and a TypeScript React page that lists them. The learner fills the design record and the API contract in the Design room's forms. Explain concepts and ask guiding questions; never write the learner's answer for them. Keep replies under 120 words and end with one question.

hints: Which stories need the API to answer something, and what does each ask for?
What does a client have to send, and what does it get back?
Which requests can fail, and how would a client tell the failures apart?
Is a book nobody has the same failure as a book already lent?
What did you choose that someone else might have chosen differently?
What would the alternative have cost?

progressive: Start with the operations: one for each thing a story needs.
Then the refusals: status and error code for each.
Finish with one decision and its reason.
